studies.title: Forgiver Of Sin, Severe In Punishment
studies.meaning: The surah opens with two disconnected letters, then a statement about where the Book comes from, then four descriptions of God set in a deliberate order: forgiver of sin, accepter of repentance, severe in punishment, holder of abundance. Two of mercy, one of severity, one of generosity, with nothing to soften the joins. Then a warning against being impressed by opponents moving prosperously about the land. Commentators read the four as one portrait rather than a list, and note that mercy stands on both sides of the severity.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah is commonly named from the third word of its third ayah. Its opening speaks to a community watching its opponents thrive: the leading families of the city were travelling, trading and gaining, and the final clause names that appearance as something not to be read as a verdict. The commentators report no specific occasion for these opening ayat.

keyTerms.note: An active participle in a possessive construction, so it names a standing description rather than an act performed on occasion. The exact phrase occurs once in the Quran, and one of this surah's names comes from it.
From a root meaning length and reach, used of a man whose means stretch far enough to be generous. As a description of God it occurs only here, closing the list on capacity rather than on threat.
A noun for turning over and shifting from one state to another, used of a sleeper turning and of goods changing hands. It names activity and prosperity without conceding that either means anything.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Meccan standing was visible in movement. A family holding shares in the caravans sent people north in summer and south in winter, and their comings and goings were the most public evidence of success anyone had. To watch the leading houses prosper while a small group of believers stayed poor was to watch an argument being won in the street, daily, without a word being said.
studies.didYouKnow: This is the first of seven consecutive surahs opening with the same two disconnected letters, from the fortieth through the forty-sixth, the longest such run in the Quran. The phrase naming God as forgiver of sin occurs only here in the whole Book, and the surah is commonly known by that word.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Setting forgiveness, acceptance of repentance, severity and abundance in one unbroken line refuses to divide God's dealings into separate departments. The reader is not offered a choice between a merciful God and a just one, since the four descriptions belong to one subject and the sentence closes by saying there is no god but He. The warning that follows applies this to history: what prospers now is not the verdict.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same warning about opponents moving prosperously in the land, with what follows for them.
Returns later in this surah to the same charge, disputing God's signs with no authority given.
Puts the forgiveness named here into the second person, addressed to those who had despaired.

studies.applyIt: Pick one person whose life looks like it is going better than yours and say silently, in plain words, what you envy about it. Then read the last clause of this passage, which names exactly that impression and tells the reader not to be taken in. The instruction is not to stop noticing. It is to stop reading a surface as a score.

studies.title: Every Community Plotted
studies.meaning: A pattern is stated rather than a story told. The people of Noah denied, and the allied parties after them; every community intended to seize its own messenger; and they argued with falsehood in order to make the truth lose its footing. Then the sentence changes person: I seized them. It closes not with a description but with a question, how was My punishment, left unanswered. Commentators note that the ayah compresses the whole prophetic history into one sentence so that the present looks like a repetition of it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, following the warning against being impressed by opponents who are prospering. This ayah supplies the reason: the same prosperity preceded every earlier collapse. The audience knew the ruined sites and the names, so the surah does not need to narrate them. One of these episodes is told at length later in the same surah, which makes this ayah its heading. No occasion is reported.

keyTerms.note: A plural for factions and confederacies. The Quran uses it of the coalitions that formed against earlier messengers, so the word carries organisation and planning rather than mere hostility.
A verb for forming an intention and moving toward it, stopping short of completing the act. It records what each community meant to do to its messenger, whether or not it managed to.
From a verb for a foot slipping on wet ground. Argument is pictured as an attempt to make the truth lose its footing, and the word occurs in only one other place in the Quran.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Seizing a man was how a dispute in that world was escalated. A troublesome person could be taken by his own kin and confined at home, handed over to an aggrieved party, or driven out with no protection at all. All three had been tried or threatened in Mecca. The word used for what every community intended toward its messenger is the ordinary one for laying hands on someone.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for making the truth lose its footing occurs twice in the Quran, here and at 18:56, and in both places it describes argument used as a tactic rather than as an attempt to find anything out. The image behind it is a foot slipping on wet clay, which is what the word means in ordinary speech.
studies.theologicalSignificance: History is presented as a pattern rather than a series of incidents, and the pattern includes the arguing as much as the violence. What earlier communities did was not only to attack their messengers but to reason badly on purpose, which the passage treats as an act rather than a failure of thinking. The abrupt shift into the first person at the end puts the outcome of every one of those episodes under one speaker.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same verb for argument aimed at unsettling the truth rather than at reaching it.
Lists the same sequence of denied messengers and closes with the same kind of question.
Names these earlier communities again later in this surah, inside a warning spoken by a believer.

studies.applyIt: Notice the next time you argue for something you already suspect is wrong, because winning is nearer than being right. Everyone does this in small ways. Stop mid-sentence once and say you need to think about it. This passage treats bad-faith argument as an action rather than an accident, which means it can be interrupted like any other action.

studies.title: Thus The Sentence Came Due
studies.meaning: A short ayah reporting an outcome rather than an event: in this way the word of your Lord became due against those who refused, that they belong with the Fire. The verb means a claim falling due, as a debt does at its term. Commentators note that nothing new is being announced. What is reported is the point at which a standing statement became applicable to particular people, which is why the sentence opens with a phrase meaning in this way and looks back to the pattern just described.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, directly after the sentence about earlier communities and how each of them ended. The surah is addressing opponents who had heard warnings for years with nothing visible happening, and this ayah speaks to the gap between a statement and its effect. The commentators read the word of the Lord here as the standing announcement about those who refuse, rather than as a fresh verdict on individuals.

keyTerms.note: From the root for truth and for a right that is owed. Applied to a statement it means the thing became actual and claimable, as a debt becomes due, rather than merely turning out to be correct.
A single utterance treated as a standing decision. The Quran uses the phrase for announcements made in advance that later apply to particular people, which is how the commentators take it here.
The word rendered companions means those who belong with a thing and keep its company, used of the people of a town or a trade. It describes association rather than a sentence imposed from outside.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Debt in Mecca ran on terms. A loan or a consignment fell due on a stated date, and until that day nothing was owed and nothing could be demanded, however certain the obligation was. The word used here comes from that vocabulary. An audience that had heard warnings for years without seeing consequences would have recognised the distinction between a claim that exists and a claim that has come due.
studies.didYouKnow: The exact phrase used here, that the word of your Lord came due, occurs twice in the Quran, here and at 10:33, where it is said of those who refuse to believe. Both places use a verb from the root meaning truth and obligation, so the statement is described as becoming owed rather than as coming to pass.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah separates a decision from its enforcement, and locates the delay in the second rather than the first. That answers a real objection, since people who are warned and see nothing happen reasonably conclude that nothing was ever going to. The passage does not argue with their observation. It reclassifies it, treating the interval as a term rather than as evidence, which is a claim about time rather than about them.

crossReferences.why: Uses the identical phrase about the word of your Lord becoming due against those who refuse.
The ayah before, whose account of earlier communities is what the phrase in this way refers back to.
Puts a closely matching admission in their own mouths at the gate, that the sentence became due.

studies.applyIt: Think of a consequence you have been told about and stopped believing in because it has not arrived: a health warning, a financial one, a strain in a relationship. Notice that you converted a delay into a disproof at some point, without deciding to. You do not need to panic about it. Just move the item back into the category it belongs in.

studies.title: Those Who Carry The Throne
studies.meaning: The ayah reports what the highest creatures are doing, and what they are doing is asking on someone else's behalf. Those who bear the Throne and those around it glorify, believe, and seek forgiveness for the believers; then their prayer is quoted directly. It opens by naming the reach of God's mercy and knowledge before making any request, and what it asks is forgiveness for those who repented and followed the path, and protection from the Blaze. Commentators note that angels are described as believing, which is unusual and deliberate.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, addressed to a small and ridiculed community. The surah has just described the parties who gathered against earlier messengers and the sentence that came due. Against that, it reports a support the believers had no way of seeing. The commentators connect this passage to the isolation of the Meccan years rather than to any particular incident, and no specific occasion is reported for the ayah.

keyTerms.note: The phrase occurs once in the Quran. The verb is the ordinary one for carrying a load, used of a person shouldering goods, and the ayah leaves it entirely without further explanation.
A verb form meaning to ask that someone's fault be covered. Its object here is other people, so the angels are described doing for believers exactly what believers are told to do for one another.
A verb for being wide enough to contain something. The prayer measures the container before asking for anything, which is why the request that follows sounds modest rather than presumptuous.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A petition to a chief was made through somebody already inside his circle, and the standing of that intermediary was the whole strength of the request. People knew precisely who could speak for them and who could not. To hear that the beings nearest the Throne were already asking on their behalf, unprompted and unpaid, described a kind of access nobody in Mecca could have arranged for themselves.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase describing those who carry the Throne occurs once in the Quran. A closely related statement at 42:5 says the angels ask forgiveness for those on the earth, and 69:17 says eight will bear the Throne of your Lord on that Day. Between them, those three passages are the whole of what the Quran says on the subject.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The prayer is quoted rather than summarised, and its order is instructive. God's mercy and knowledge are named first, then forgiveness is asked for a defined group: those who repented and followed the path. Nothing is requested for anyone in general. The passage also shows the highest creatures believing rather than merely obeying, which puts faith at the centre of creation instead of treating it as a human peculiarity.

crossReferences.why: Says the angels glorify their Lord and ask forgiveness for those on the earth, in nearly the same terms.
Describes the bearing of the Throne on that Day, with angels ranged around its borders.
Continues the same prayer two ayat later, asking that they be shielded from evil deeds.

studies.applyIt: Ask God's forgiveness once today for someone else by name, and do not tell them you did. The prayer quoted here is made by beings who gain nothing from it, for people who never hear it. Try that shape once: a name, a request, no audience. Most people find it changes how they think about the person afterwards.

studies.title: And The Righteous Among Their Families
studies.meaning: The prayer continues and widens. Admit them to the Gardens of lasting residence which You promised them, and whoever was upright among their parents, their spouses and their offspring. The qualifying clause is the interesting part. The family are included, but on condition of their own uprightness, so nothing is being asked by association. Commentators note that the promise is treated as already made, which is why the prayer asks for its keeping rather than for a new favour, and that the family clause is an addition beyond it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Faith in that city cut through households: some believers had parents who opposed them, some had children who did not follow, and marriages were strained or broken by it. A prayer naming parents, spouses and offspring in a single line speaks straight into that situation. The commentators report no specific occasion for the ayah, and a closely parallel promise appears at 13:23.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to stay put and settle, the same one behind the word for a mineral vein fixed in the ground. It describes permanence of dwelling rather than pleasure, and appears eleven times in the Quran.
The plain verb behind the word for righteous deeds, whose root sense is a thing being in good working order. It is used of a repaired tool as readily as of a person's conduct.
A word covering children and every descendant after them, from a root suggesting scattering or sowing. It extends the prayer forward through generations the people praying will never meet.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A household in Mecca was an economic and legal unit, not only a family. Its members shared protection, standing and liability, and a man's fortunes reached his parents, his wife and his children whether they wanted them to or not. The idea that entry to a place might run along household lines was intuitive to that audience. The condition attached here, that they be upright themselves, cuts directly against it.
studies.didYouKnow: The same three relations, parents, spouses and offspring, appear together in a promise at 13:23, worded so closely that the commentators read the two passages side by side. Here the words are a request made by angels; there they are a statement of what will happen, so the same content stands once as prayer and once as promise.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two things usually kept apart are held together. The bond of a family is honoured, since the prayer names them by relation and asks for them as such, and personal responsibility is preserved, since the request covers only those who were upright. Nobody is admitted on a relative's account and nobody is excluded for lacking one. The prayer also asks for what was already promised, treating a promise as something worth asking to see kept.

crossReferences.why: States as a promise what this ayah asks as a prayer, naming the same three family relations.
Describes offspring joined to those who believed, with nobody's own work reduced for it.
The first half of the same prayer, asking forgiveness for those who repented and followed the path.

studies.applyIt: Say a prayer today that names three people in your family aloud, one from each generation you can reach: someone older, someone your own age, someone younger. The prayer in this ayah is specific about relations rather than vague about loved ones, and saying actual names changes how the asking feels while you are doing it.

studies.title: Shield Them From The Evils
studies.meaning: The angels' prayer closes with a request and then a definition. Shield them from evil deeds; and whoever You shield from evil deeds on that Day, You have shown mercy to him. The second clause is not a repetition. It states what mercy consists of in this setting, and it turns out to be protection from a person's own record rather than the granting of anything. The final words then name the whole thing the great triumph. Commentators note that the verb for shielding shares its root with the word usually rendered God-consciousness.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, closing the prayer begun two ayat earlier. The surah is speaking to people whose situation offered them no protection of the ordinary kind, and the prayer they are shown asks for protection of an entirely different order. The commentators treat these three ayat as one quoted supplication and note that this final clause is the only line in it that explains itself.

keyTerms.note: An imperative from the verb for putting something between a person and harm. The same root gives the word usually translated God-consciousness, so the prayer asks God to do what a person is elsewhere told to do.
A plural covering bad actions and the harms that follow from them, so the request reads either as protection from the deeds or from their consequences, and the commentators keep both open.
A word joining winning and escaping danger in one root. Calling the outcome a triumph rather than a reward frames the whole matter as something survived rather than something collected.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Protection in Arabia was a formal relationship with a name, invoked in ordinary speech every day. A man under someone's protection could travel and trade safely; losing it left him exposed with no recourse and no court. The verb in this prayer belongs to that world, and the audience would have heard the angels asking God to extend protection in exactly the sense a clan extended it to a client.
studies.didYouKnow: The same verb for shielding appears twice within this short prayer, once at the end of the previous ayah and once at the start of this one: first asking protection from the Blaze, then from the evil deeds themselves. The prayer moves backward from the punishment to its cause, which reverses the order people usually pray in.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Mercy is given a definition here rather than an adjective. Being shielded from your own evil deeds on that Day is what having been shown mercy amounts to, which locates mercy in the lifting of a liability rather than in the giving of a gift. The word chosen for the outcome then recasts the whole hereafter as an escape rather than a prize, which is a sober note on which to end a prayer.

crossReferences.why: Begins this same prayer, asking forgiveness for those who repented and followed God's path.
Uses the same root for the outcome: whoever is kept away from the Fire and admitted has triumphed.
Goes beyond shielding, describing bad deeds exchanged outright for good ones after repentance.

studies.applyIt: Before you next ask God for something you want, ask first to be kept from the harm inside something you have already done. The prayer here puts protection from your own record ahead of every other request, which is an unusual order. Try it once in your own words and notice how much shorter the rest of the list becomes.

studies.title: Greater Than Your Own Loathing
studies.meaning: A sentence is called out to those who refused, and it works entirely by comparison. God's loathing is greater than your loathing of yourselves, and the ground for it is given in the same breath: you were called to faith and you refused. Commentators note that the self-loathing is assumed rather than argued for, since the people addressed have already reached the point of hating what they did. The ayah introduces no new emotion. It takes one they have and tells them their estimate of it is small.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in a passage describing the moment after arrival. The surah has just quoted the prayer of the angels, and this is its exact reverse: an address to those for whom nobody asked. The commentators read the calling out as public, since the verb used is the one for a proclamation cried to a crowd rather than a message delivered privately. No occasion is reported.

keyTerms.note: A verb for calling across a distance, used of a herald or of someone shouting to a caravan. It is public and one-directional, and the passive form leaves the speaker entirely unnamed.
A strong noun for settled disgust at something contemptible, colder than anger and more lasting. The Quran uses it of actions people find repellent rather than of enemies they are fighting.
The verb behind the word for rejection, whose root sense is covering something over. The tense makes it habitual, so what is named is a repeated response rather than one decision taken once.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Public proclamation was how a verdict was made real. A herald announced a decision at the assembly or in the market so that everyone heard it at the same moment, and the shame of a judgement lay as much in its being cried aloud as in its content. The verb here belongs to that practice, and the audience would have pictured a crier rather than a quiet word.
studies.didYouKnow: The comparison in this ayah is between two instances of a single word, God's loathing and their loathing of themselves, a construction the Quran uses sparingly. The same word returns later in this surah, at 40:35, where disputing God's signs without any authority is called a great loathing in the sight of God and of those who believe.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage assumes self-reproach is already present and treats it as accurate but too small, which is a distinctive move. It does not tell the people addressed that they are wrong to hate what they did; it tells them they have underestimated. The reason given is also narrow and precise. What is named is not a set of beliefs but one repeated act: being called, and refusing.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same word for loathing, there of disputing God's signs with no authority for it.
Applies the same term to the gap between what people say and what they actually do.
The reply of those addressed, who acknowledge their sins and ask whether there is a way out.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you did that you already dislike yourself for. You do not need to add anything to that feeling today. Just notice that this ayah treats it as a real measurement that happens to fall short, and that what it points toward is not more self-reproach but the thing that was being refused.

studies.title: Two Deaths And Two Lives
studies.meaning: The answer given is a confession followed by a question. They state what has happened to them in the plainest arithmetic, two deaths and two lives, then acknowledge their sins, then ask whether there is any way out. Commentators explain the count in more than one way, most reading the first death as the state before existing and the second as ordinary dying, with the two lives being this one and the raising. What the ayah stages is a full admission arriving too late to be repentance, offered instead as a bargaining position.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Being raised after death was the sticking point in the city's argument with the message, and this ayah answers it by having the deniers themselves recite the sequence as fact. A closely matching arithmetic appears at 2:28, where the same four stages are set out as a rebuke to people who deny God. No specific occasion is reported for the ayah.

keyTerms.note: The number stands alone without a noun, so it counts occurrences of the verb rather than people. The construction is compact enough that the commentators built several different readings on it.

A verb for acknowledging something openly, from a root connected with knowing and recognising. Confession here is presented as new information about themselves, offered as though it might still count for something.
The plain noun for going out, used of leaving a house or a town. Its ordinariness is the point: what is asked for is a door, and the request is left without any answer.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Confession carried weight in that society. A man who admitted a wrong before witnesses could expect the matter settled at a rate, and admitting fault early was a recognised way of reducing what you would owe. The move made in this ayah is exactly that move, made at the wrong moment. The audience would have recognised both the tactic and the reason it fails here.
studies.didYouKnow: The arithmetic here is spoken by the deniers themselves, while the same sequence appears at 2:28 as a question put to them: you were dead and He gave you life, then He causes you to die, then He gives you life. The two passages set out an identical progression from opposite directions, one as challenge and one as admission.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage stages a complete admission and then shows that admission is not the same as turning back. Everything the message asked for is granted here: the sequence acknowledged, the sins named, the authority accepted without argument. What is missing is only the time, and the ayah lets that absence do all the work. Sincerity, it implies, is not the whole of repentance, and the timing is part of the thing itself.

crossReferences.why: Sets out the identical sequence of death and life as a question put to those who deny God.
Shows the same request made at the point of death, and says plainly why it changes nothing.
Gives the answer to their question, naming what they did when God alone was called upon.

studies.applyIt: Think of an apology you have been delaying. Apologies work partly because of when they arrive; the same words are a different act at a different time. Without dwelling on it, send one today that you were going to send eventually anyway. The passage is about a confession that came too late to be anything, and yours has not.

studies.title: When God Alone Was Called
studies.meaning: The reply to their question is a diagnosis rather than a refusal. This is because when God was called on by Himself you rejected it, and when others were associated with Him you believed. Two clauses describe the same people responding to two versions of the same claim, and the only variable is exclusivity. Commentators note that belief is described here as something they were fully capable of, and that it appeared the moment the demand for exclusivity was dropped. The ayah closes by placing the judgement with God.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The people addressed were not without religion; devotion in the city was plural and enthusiastic, and their objection to the message was to what it excluded rather than to what it affirmed. The commentators read this ayah as identifying precisely that. It restates in the second person what the previous surah described from outside. No occasion is reported.

keyTerms.note: The word for singleness stands last, where Arabic places the item under emphasis. What was rejected is located exactly in that final word rather than in the calling upon God itself.
A passive from the word for taking a business partner into a venture. The passive leaves the associating without an agent, which quietly separates the act from any particular person performing it.
A noun covering a verdict, the authority to decide, and wisdom together. Placing it with God at the close answers the question asked in the previous ayah without addressing it directly at all.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Religion in Mecca was inclusive by design. The sanctuary held many objects of devotion, pilgrims arrived from tribes with their own, and adding a figure cost nothing while removing one insulted somebody. A message that asked only for addition would have been absorbed without friction. The single thing the arrangement could not accommodate was a claim that admitted nothing beside itself.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah puts into the second person what 39:45 describes from outside, where the hearts of those who do not believe in the hereafter contract when God alone is mentioned and brighten when others are named. The two passages stand in consecutive surahs and use the same word for alone in the same emphatic position.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The diagnosis is unusual because it grants the capacity while refusing the terms. These people could believe, and did believe; the ayah says so plainly. What they would not accept was a claim leaving no room for anything else, and the passage treats that as the whole of the matter. It relocates refusal from an inability to a preference, which is harder to answer and much closer to most people's experience.

crossReferences.why: Describes the same reaction from outside, hearts contracting when God alone is mentioned.
The question this ayah answers, put by people looking for a door out of where they are.
Sets out the position being rejected here, devotion offered through intermediaries said to bring people nearer.

studies.applyIt: Notice one place where you accept a demanding idea in principle but quietly keep an exemption for yourself. Everyone runs at least one. Name it in a single sentence without resolving to fix it today. This ayah describes people who agreed with everything except the part that excluded their alternatives, and naming your exemption is most of the work.

studies.title: Call On Him With Devotion
studies.meaning: Two ayat, the first giving a reason and the second drawing a conclusion. God shows you His signs and sends down provision from the sky, and only the one who keeps turning back takes any of it in. Then the instruction: call on God with your devotion made purely His, even though those who refuse dislike it. Commentators note the order carefully. Evidence is available to everyone and lands only on someone already turning, so signs are not treated as arguments that compel but as things a certain disposition can read.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, immediately after the exchange with those who asked for a way out. The instruction to call on God sincerely whatever the opposition thinks was given to a community whose devotions were conducted in a city that resented them and said so. The final clause names that resentment directly rather than promising it will end. No specific occasion is reported for either ayah.

keyTerms.note: A verb for coming back to where you belong, in a form implying habit rather than a single act. Taking heed is therefore attributed to someone already in the practice of returning.
From a root for a thing being separated out until nothing foreign remains in it, used of butter clarified or metal refined. Sincerity here is a purity of content rather than a strength of feeling.
A word covering religion, obedience owed, and the reckoning of debts. What is to be kept pure is therefore the whole relation of service, not only the intention behind a particular act.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Rain in that country was the clearest thing a person could point at. It arrived from a direction nobody controlled, it made the difference between a year and a famine, and no one claimed to have produced it. Calling provision something sent down from the sky was not a figure of speech to that audience. It was a plain description of how food actually reached them.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase about making devotion purely God's occurs seven times in the Quran, and twice inside this surah, here and again at 40:65. Both times in this surah it is an imperative, and neither time is a reward attached to it: once it is followed by the resentment of others, and once by praise of the Lord of the Worlds.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two claims sit together here. Evidence is universally available and selectively effective, which places the difference between people in their disposition rather than in their information. And devotion is to be kept pure regardless of who resents it, which detaches sincerity from social approval. Read together they describe a practice that depends neither on persuading others nor on being welcomed by them.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same instruction to serve God with devotion made purely His, at the head of that surah.
Repeats the identical phrase later in this surah, joined there to God being the Living One.
Shows the same sincerity appearing under pressure at sea and disappearing again on dry land.

studies.applyIt: Do one act of devotion today that nobody will know about and that gains you nothing socially: two extra units of prayer, a charity given without a name attached, a supplication for someone who will never hear it. The word this passage uses is about content rather than feeling, so what matters is only that no second motive is mixed in.

studies.title: He Casts The Spirit
studies.meaning: Three descriptions and one action. God is exalted in degrees and owner of the Throne, and He casts the spirit of His command upon whomever He wills of His servants, so that he may warn of the Day of Meeting. Commentators differ over what the spirit means here, most reading it as revelation itself and some as the angel who brings it, and they record the range. What the ayah settles is the purpose. Revelation is sent to warn, and the day it warns of is named by an encounter rather than by a verdict.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The city's objection was not that God existed but that He had chosen this particular man, and the ayah answers by describing selection as something God does rather than something a person qualifies for. The name given to the coming day occurs nowhere else in the Quran, and the commentators explain it as the meeting of creatures with their Lord and of people with their own deeds.

keyTerms.note: A phrase occurring once in the Quran. The second word means steps or ranks, so the description places God above every level rather than at the top of one, and commentators read it both ways.
Commentators read it here as revelation, as the angel who brings revelation, or as what gives life to hearts. The Quran uses the word in all three senses, and this ayah does not narrow it.
A verbal noun of a form meaning two parties meeting each other, so the encounter is mutual. It occurs once in the Quran, naming the Day by a relation rather than by an outcome.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: An appointed meeting was a serious matter in a world with no dates written down. Parties to a dispute agreed a place and a season and travelled to it; a caravan and its escort met at a fixed watering point on an agreed day. The word used for the coming Day belongs to that world of arranged encounters, and calling it a meeting rather than a reckoning changes what a listener pictures.
studies.didYouKnow: This surah gives the coming Day three names that are rare or unique in the Quran: the Day of Meeting here, the Day of Imminence at 40:18, and the Day of Calling Out at 40:32. The description of God that opens this ayah, exalted in degrees, is also found nowhere else in the Book.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Selection is described without a criterion. God casts the spirit upon whom He wills of His servants, and no qualification is named, which removes the argument the city was having about whether this particular man deserved it. The purpose clause then narrows the function sharply: to warn. Revelation is not presented here as information or as comfort in the first place, but as notice given before an appointment nobody made for themselves.

crossReferences.why: Says He sends down the angels with the spirit by His command upon whom He wills of His servants.
Describes revelation as a spirit sent by God's command to someone who did not know the Book.
Gives the same coming Day another of this surah's rare names, the Day of Imminence.

studies.applyIt: Say the phrase Day of Meeting to yourself once and notice that it is not a frightening name. Meetings are arranged, expected, and attended by both parties. Then pick one thing you would like to have done by then, small enough to begin this week, and treat it as preparation for an appointment rather than as insurance against a threat.

studies.title: To Whom Belongs The Kingdom
studies.meaning: A day is named by what people are: out in the open, with nothing about them hidden from God. Then a question is asked with no speaker identified, to whom does the kingdom belong today, and it is answered with no speaker identified either. Commentators say the question is put and answered by God Himself, since by then nobody else is in a position to reply. The answer uses two names together, the One and the Overpowering, a pairing the Quran uses six times and always where power admits no rival.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Sovereignty in the city belonged to a few families and was displayed constantly: in the custody of hereditary offices, in the seating at the assembly, in who spoke first and who waited. The question asked in this ayah is exactly the question those arrangements answered every day. Setting it in a place where nobody can claim anything is the whole point. No occasion is reported.

keyTerms.note: From a verb meaning to come out into open ground, used of a champion stepping forward from the ranks. It occurs once in the Quran and describes people out of cover rather than merely visible.
Ownership joined to the right to command, the word used of a king's authority over territory. The question uses the definite form, so what is asked about is the whole of it rather than a share.
An intensive form from a verb meaning to subdue something completely. Paired with the One, it says that oneness here is not a count but a condition in which nothing else holds power.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Rank was physical and constantly on display. Where a man sat in the assembly, who walked ahead of whom in a narrow street, which family held the keys and the watering rights: all of it was visible and none of it was in doubt. A question asked aloud about who holds authority would have sounded to that audience like a challenge issued in a public place, of a kind that occasionally happened and always mattered.
studies.didYouKnow: The pairing of the One and the Overpowering occurs six times in the Quran, and every one of them stands in a passage arguing against divided sovereignty. One of the six is spoken by a prisoner to his fellow inmates at 12:39. The question in this ayah is unusual in having no named speaker on either side of it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah stages a moment when a live question receives its answer with nobody left to dispute it. What is striking is that the question is asked at all, since by then the answer cannot be in doubt. Asking it aloud converts a fact into an acknowledgement, and the passage seems to be inviting the reader to make that acknowledgement early, while the question can still be answered wrongly.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same pair of names in a prison, contrasting scattered lords with the One, the Overpowering.
Describes the same day, when no soul can do anything for another and the command is God's.
States that true sovereignty on that Day belongs to the Merciful, and that it is a hard day.

studies.applyIt: Answer the question in this ayah out loud today, in the ordinary conditions of your life rather than under pressure. Then notice one small place where your day is arranged as though the answer were something else: a person whose approval you organise around, a fear you obey without thinking. You are not being asked to fix it, only to see the gap.

studies.title: No Injustice On That Day
studies.meaning: Three short statements in a row. Today every soul is repaid for what it earned; there is no wrong today; God is swift in reckoning. The middle clause is a flat denial rather than a promise, which is a different kind of assurance from the one people usually look for. The last is commonly read as being about speed, and the commentators add a second sense: an account settled quickly is one where nothing needs working out, because everything is already known. No punishment or reward is described.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, following straight on from the question about who holds sovereignty. The order matters: authority is established first, and only then is its exercise described. The audience knew what unchecked authority looked like, since arbitration in the city depended on the standing of the parties nearly as much as on the merits of a case. The commentators report no specific occasion for the ayah.

keyTerms.note: A passive verb for giving what corresponds to a thing done, used of wages and of returning a favour. It covers reward and penalty in one word, so the sentence names the mechanism without naming any outcome.
The root sense is putting a thing where it does not belong, and the same root gives the word for darkness. Denying it here denies misplacement of any kind rather than only harshness.
A phrase occurring eight times in the Quran. Commentators read the speed as a consequence of complete knowledge, since an account that needs no investigation can be settled at once.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A reckoning at the end of a season took days. Ledgers were compared, witnesses called, disputed items argued over, and a powerful party could stretch the process out until the weaker one gave up and accepted less. Everyone had watched an account settled slowly and unfairly. The two claims in this ayah, no wrong and no delay, answer the two ways such an audience knew a reckoning could fail.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase calling God swift in reckoning occurs eight times in the Quran and never in isolation; it always closes a passage about accountability. Here it follows a flat denial that there will be any wrong at all, which makes the speed a consequence of complete knowledge rather than a threat about how little time remains.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Justice is stated negatively, as the absence of misplacement, which claims less and delivers more than a positive description would. The ayah does not say everyone receives what they hoped for; it says nothing will be put where it does not belong. Taken with the previous ayah about sovereignty, the passage makes a particular point: absolute authority and exact justice are asserted of one being, and neither is qualified by the other.

crossReferences.why: Describes scales set for that Day, with no soul wronged even by a mustard seed's weight.
Closes a long passage with the same assurance of full payment and no wrong done to anyone.
The ayah before, which establishes whose authority is being exercised in this reckoning.

studies.applyIt: Think of one time you were on the wrong end of a decision made by somebody with more power than you, and identify the specific part that still stings. It is usually the misplacement rather than the loss itself. Read the middle clause of this ayah with that in mind. It is a denial of exactly that, and it is stated without qualification.

studies.title: The Treachery Of The Eyes
studies.meaning: A warning, and then a turn inward with no transition. Warn them of a day that has drawn close, when hearts are up at the throats and stifled, and the wrongdoers have no intimate friend and no intercessor who is obeyed. Then: He knows the treachery of the eyes and what the breasts conceal. Commentators explain the phrase about eyes as the stolen glance, the look given when nobody is watching, and note the deliberate change of scale, from a day of terror to a single movement of the eye.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah has been describing a public reckoning, and here it names the private material that reckoning will work on. The phrase used for the day is one of several rare names this surah gives it. The commentators do not report a specific occasion; later readers sometimes attached the phrase about glances to particular incidents, but the classical commentaries keep it general, as the ayah does.

keyTerms.note: An active participle from a verb meaning to draw very close, used of a departure time almost arrived. It occurs twice in the Quran, naming the Day by its nearness rather than by its content.
The anatomical word for the upper throat. It occurs twice in the Quran, here and of believers besieged at Medina, so the same physical description covers terror in both settings.
A phrase occurring once in the whole Quran. Commentators explain it as the stolen look, the glance a person gives while believing that nobody can see them give it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Meccan life left very little unobserved. Households shared courtyards, business was done in the open, and reputations were built and lost in front of witnesses who remembered. The one thing a person could keep entirely to himself was where his eyes went. That was the last unpoliced space available, and this passage names it directly rather than speaking generally about hidden things.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase about the treachery of the eyes occurs once in the whole Quran. The image of hearts reaching the throats occurs twice, here and at 33:10, where it describes believers under siege in an actual battle, so the same bodily description is used for fear on the Day and for fear in a trench outside Medina.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage sets the largest scale beside the smallest without comment: a day when hearts are in throats, and a glance nobody saw. Putting them in adjacent sentences makes a claim about the resolution of the reckoning, that it does not work only on the scale of major deeds. It also explains the clause just before it about having no intercessor who is obeyed, since the record includes what nobody else was ever able to report.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same image of hearts reaching the throats, there of believers besieged in a real battle.
Names the same coming event with the same rare word, saying the imminent has drawn near.
Addresses the same faculty this ayah says is known, telling believing men to restrain their looks.

studies.applyIt: For one hour today, notice where your eyes go when you are not thinking about it. Do not correct anything and do not make a rule out of it. Just observe which way your attention turns when it is off the leash. This passage names that exact zone as known, and one honest hour of noticing is the whole exercise.

studies.title: They Decide Nothing At All
studies.meaning: A contrast in two clauses, then a pair of names. God decides with the truth, and those they call on besides Him decide nothing whatever. The same verb governs both halves, which is what makes the sentence work: the other objects of devotion are measured on the one function at issue and found to perform none of it. The two names that close the ayah, the Hearing and the Seeing, are read by commentators as the requirements for judging, since a judge must take in the evidence before he can decide anything.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, closing the passage about the reckoning. The surah has described a day of exposure, an exact repayment and a knowledge reaching as far as a private glance. This ayah asks what else could conceivably do that work and answers with a flat nothing. The commentators attach the two names at the end to the act of judging rather than reading them as a general formula. No occasion is reported.

keyTerms.note: A verb covering giving a verdict, settling a matter and finishing something off. The same word governs both halves of this ayah, which makes the comparison exact rather than merely rhetorical.
An indefinite noun standing under a negation, which is the strongest denial Arabic has. It rules out not only major decisions but any decision whatever, down to the smallest one.
Two intensive forms naming permanent capacities rather than acts. Placed after a statement about judging, they supply exactly what a judge needs: testimony taken in, and the scene itself observed.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: An arbitrator's authority rested on his capacity to hear both parties and to see the thing in dispute, and cases were routinely moved to a man who could do both. A judge who was absent, or who took his evidence at second hand, was distrusted for that reason alone. The two names closing this ayah name the qualifications that an audience of litigants would have listed first.
studies.didYouKnow: The two verbs in this ayah come from a single root, so the Arabic reads as one word applied twice, once affirmed of God and once denied of everything else. The pair of names at the end occurs several times in the Quran, and here it is attached directly to a statement about judging rather than to one about knowledge in general.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The argument is conducted entirely on function. Nothing is said about what the other objects of devotion are made of, who made them, or what anyone believes about them. They are asked to perform one task and they perform none of it. That keeps the case narrow and testable, and it locates the divine names in what they enable rather than in what they assert, since hearing and seeing are named because judging requires them.

crossReferences.why: Tests them on a far smaller task, whether they could create a fly or recover what it takes.
Makes the same functional argument about intercession, which belongs entirely to God.
Establishes whose the sovereignty is, which this ayah then applies to the act of judging.

studies.applyIt: Take one decision you are stuck on and list, honestly, who or what you are actually waiting on to settle it: a person's opinion, a market, an outcome. Then ask which of them will in fact decide it. Usually one or two names come off the list immediately. This ayah works by putting exactly that question to a much larger case.

studies.theme: Time and the Brevity of Life
studies.title: Stronger, And Left More Traces
studies.meaning: A question that is really an instruction: have they not travelled the earth and looked at how those before them ended. Then a comparison that concedes everything to the past. They were stronger, and they left more marks on the ground. Commentators note that the ayah grants the opponents' own standard, since Meccan confidence rested on strength and on visible works, and then reports what became of people who had more of both. The closing clause carries the point: they had no protector against God.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The trade routes north and south ran past the remains of older civilisations, and Meccan merchants passed them twice a year on the summer and winter journeys. The surah appeals to that direct experience rather than to a report someone had heard. Closely similar ayat appear at 30:9 and 35:44, so the argument was made more than once in this period. No occasion is reported.

keyTerms.note: The ordinary verb for going about the land, from the root behind the word for a life's course or a biography. Looking is joined to it, so the instruction is to travel with attention rather than only to move.
Marks left by something that has passed, used of footprints and of ruins. It concedes to the earlier peoples the very thing a builder is proudest of, the standing evidence that they were here.
An active participle from the verb for placing something between a person and harm, the same root used in the angels' prayer earlier in this surah. Here the word is denied instead of requested.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The road north toward Syria passed rock-cut facades carved into cliffs by a people the Quran names elsewhere, still standing and empty. Meccan traders saw them with their own eyes on the summer route. Nobody in that audience needed to be told that a civilisation could vanish and leave its architecture behind. They had ridden past the evidence since childhood, until it had become ordinary.
studies.didYouKnow: This argument is made in almost identical words three times in the Quran, here and at 30:9 and 35:44. Each time it is a question about travelling and looking, and each time it concedes that the earlier peoples were stronger. It is one of the few arguments in the Quran that points at physical evidence the audience could go and inspect for themselves.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage takes the opponents' own measure of success and uses it without disputing it. The strength was real, the works were real, and the traces are still visible. What is denied is only that any of it functioned as protection. That leaves a reader's assessment of worldly achievement intact while removing its security value, which is a narrower and far more durable point than saying the achievements did not matter.

crossReferences.why: Puts the same question in nearly the same words, adding that they cultivated the land more.
Asks it again, closing with the note that nothing frustrates God in the heavens or the earth.
Uses the same word for a protector, denying any defender against God to those who do wrong.

studies.applyIt: Look at a picture of somewhere that used to matter and no longer does: a closed factory, a former office, a family house sold years ago. Spend a minute on it without slipping into nostalgia. This ayah asks its audience to travel and look, and the modern version of that errand is available on your phone in under a minute.

studies.title: A Lying Sorcerer, They Said
studies.meaning: A general statement and then a specific case. Their messengers used to come to them with clear proofs and they refused, so God seized them. Then the pattern is illustrated: Moses was sent with signs and a clear authority to Pharaoh, to his minister, and to a wealthy man of his own people, and the three of them answered with two words, a lying sorcerer. Commentators note the compression. The whole encounter is reduced to what was sent and what was said back, and the reply is an accusation of fraud rather than an argument.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The same charge of sorcery was being made in the city against the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), which is why this episode is chosen and told in these terms. The three names are given without explanation, since the audience already knew who they were. This is the opening of the longest sustained narrative in the surah, and no specific occasion is reported for the ayat themselves.

keyTerms.note: A plural for things that make a matter plain, used of evidence that settles a dispute. It describes what the messengers brought as demonstration rather than as assertion, which is what the reply then has to deal with.

The first word means power and the warrant to exercise it, and the Quran uses it of evidence that establishes a claim. The phrase occurs nine times, sometimes of what a messenger is given and sometimes of what opponents are challenged to produce.

Two intensive nouns side by side with no connective, so each strengthens the other. The first names a technique and the second a character, which is how the charge worked: not mistaken, but working a trick.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Sorcery was a recognised craft with recognised effects, not a superstition to be laughed at. People paid for charms, for knots blown upon, for words said over a sick child. Calling someone a sorcerer therefore explained an inexplicable event without conceding anything at all: the thing happened, and it was a technique. It was the cheapest way to acknowledge a sign and dismiss it in the same breath.
studies.didYouKnow: The three figures named in this passage appear together in only one other place in the Quran, at 29:39, where the same three are said to have been approached by Moses with clear proofs and to have behaved arrogantly. Pharaoh's minister is named six times in the Quran, and never once apart from Pharaoh himself.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage identifies a way of refusing that is not disbelief in the ordinary sense. Nothing is denied. The signs are granted as having happened and then reclassified as a trick, a move that requires no evidence and cannot be answered by producing more signs. That is why the narrative which follows turns on speech and courage rather than on further demonstration. An accusation of fraud closes a question instead of asking one.

crossReferences.why: Names the same three figures together, the only other place in the Quran where they appear as a group.
Reports the same charge against Moses in nearly the same words, a sorcerer or a madman.
Shows what the accusation licensed two ayat later, when Pharaoh proposes killing him.

studies.applyIt: Notice the next time you dismiss something by naming it rather than answering it: that is just marketing, that is just politics, that is only how they were brought up. The naming may well be correct. Ask yourself once, honestly, whether you reached for it because it was true or because it saved you a conversation.

studies.title: Kill The Sons Of Believers
studies.meaning: The order given is precise, and it is not aimed at Moses. Kill the sons of those who have believed with him, and let their women live. Commentators note that a similar policy is described earlier in his life, before he was sent, so what is reported here is its renewal against a group defined by belief rather than by descent. The ayah then steps outside the scene entirely: the scheming of those who refuse comes to nothing. The judgement is passed on the plan, not on the suffering.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, told to a community under pressure of its own kind. The commentators connect this narrative to the position of the believers in Mecca, some of whom were being held, beaten or starved by their own families. The comparison was not exact and was not meant to be. What the passage supplies is the shape of a situation in which the powerful answer a message with force against the weakest people near it.

keyTerms.note: A verb meaning to keep alive, from the root for life, which also gives the word for modesty. Here it names the sparing of the daughters, which was not mercy but the other half of one policy.
A word for a plan made quietly against someone, covering trickery and manoeuvre together. Calling this a stratagem frames it as an attempt at an outcome, which is what the ayah then says fails.
The same word used for being lost in open country and for being religiously misguided. Saying the plan is in error rather than defeated says it was never on a route to anywhere at all.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A community's future was its sons. Sons carried the name, fought, inherited and negotiated, and a group that lost a generation of them was absorbed by others within a lifetime. Killing the boys and sparing the girls was not random cruelty but a recognised way of ending a people without killing all of them, and the audience understood precisely what was being described.
studies.didYouKnow: The same policy is described at 2:49 and 7:127, where it is directed at a people identified by descent. In this ayah the group is defined differently, as those who believed with him, so the target has moved from a lineage to a conviction. That shift is what makes this version the one told to a small believing community in Mecca.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The closing clause claims something the scene itself does not yet show: the scheming comes to nothing. Nothing in the narrative at this point demonstrates the plan failing, and the children are not said to be spared. What is asserted is that the plan was never a route to the outcome it wanted, which is a statement about the structure of events rather than a consolation about this one. The suffering is left standing and unexplained.

crossReferences.why: Describes the same policy against the same people, called there a tremendous trial from their Lord.
Reports the decision being taken in council, with the same two halves of the order given.
States the same principle about scheming, that God's planning outlasts the plans made by others.

studies.applyIt: If you are in the middle of something unjust that shows no sign of ending, notice carefully what this ayah does and does not say. It does not say the harm is small or that it will stop soon. It says the plan behind it is not on a road to anywhere. Hold those two things separately today, without collapsing either into the other.

studies.title: Leave Me To Kill Moses
studies.meaning: A short speech that is entirely about how it sounds. Leave me to kill him, and let him call on his Lord; I fear he will change your religion or cause corruption to appear in the land. Commentators note the opening, where a man with absolute power asks to be released, which is a performance of restraint. The killing is then justified twice, as protecting religion and as preventing disorder, and both reasons are given as fears. Nothing in the speech is presented as what the speaker wants.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The city's leadership had been making similar arguments about the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him): that he was dividing families, insulting the sanctuary and threatening arrangements everybody depended on. The commentators read this episode as chosen for that resemblance. Causing corruption in the land was a standard charge in Arabian political speech, and the audience recognised the register at once.

keyTerms.note: An imperative meaning let me alone to do it. It occurs once in the Quran, and it presents a decision already taken as though it were being held back by others who must now release it.
The ordinary verb for being afraid. Putting the case in this form converts an intention into an anxiety, which is exactly what makes the sentence sound protective rather than aggressive.
From a root meaning a thing going bad, as food spoils. Used politically it covers unrest and the breakdown of arrangements, and it was the standard charge brought against anyone unsettling an order.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Public speech in that world was made before a council, and a leader who wanted a dangerous thing done well presented it as a reluctance finally overcome. Chiefs consulted, or appeared to consult. The formula of asking to be released to do what you have already decided was recognisable rhetoric, and the people hearing this surah had heard versions of it from their own leaders within living memory.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase Pharaoh uses to open this speech occurs once in the whole Quran. The charge he brings, that Moses will make corruption appear in the land, is the same accusation the Quran records being made repeatedly against believers, and at 2:11 and 2:12 it is turned back onto the people making it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage records how violence is talked about rather than how it is done. Three moves are made in a single sentence: permission is requested, the target is dismissed by inviting him to call for help, and the killing is dressed as a defence of religion and of public order. The Quran quotes it without adding a comment, which leaves the reader to notice the structure. Recognising that structure is the use the passage has.

crossReferences.why: Records the same charge of causing corruption and reverses it onto the people making it.
Has his own council make a version of the argument, that Moses will cause trouble in the land.
The reply, which does not answer the argument but names the thing standing behind it.

studies.applyIt: Listen this week for the sentence that presents a decision already made as a reluctant duty: I have no choice, it is for everyone's good, I am worried about what happens otherwise. You will hear it in ordinary places. Notice the shape rather than judging the speaker, and then check whether you use it yourself.

studies.title: I Have Sought Refuge
studies.meaning: The reply is one sentence and it does not engage the argument at all. I have taken refuge in my Lord and your Lord from every arrogant one who does not believe in the Day of Account. Commentators note the two possessives, my Lord and your Lord, which refuses the assumption that the dispute is between two gods. The threat is generalised as well. Moses does not name the man in front of him; he names a type, and the defining feature he gives is not cruelty but the absence of belief in a reckoning.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Taking refuge was a formal act with legal weight in Arabia: a person under threat could seek the protection of a household or a sanctuary and be safe inside it. Moses is described using exactly that vocabulary, with God as the protector. The community hearing this had watched some of its own members seek and then lose that kind of protection in Mecca. No occasion is reported.

keyTerms.note: A verb for putting yourself under someone's protection, from the root behind the words said when seeking shelter from harm. It occurs twice in the Quran, and both times it is spoken by Moses.
One who makes himself great, and indefinite here, so it names a type rather than a person. The Quran uses the same word for the class named at the gate in its scenes of judgement.
Literally the day of the reckoning up, using the word for arithmetic and for settling a ledger. Naming it as what the arrogant do not believe in makes that disbelief the root of the behaviour.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Seeking protection was done with a formula and in public. A man in danger went to a chief or to a sanctuary and declared himself under protection, and the declaration bound the protector's honour in front of witnesses. Refusing it was shameful and violating it was worse. When Moses says he has taken refuge, the audience heard a legal act being performed rather than a private feeling being expressed.
studies.didYouKnow: This verb for taking refuge occurs twice in the Quran, and both times it is spoken by Moses: here, and at 44:20, where he says he has taken refuge in his Lord and yours lest they stone him. The two sentences are nearly identical, and both name God with the same double possessive, my Lord and your Lord.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The reply reframes the danger without denying it. The threat is real, and the response is not defiance but shelter, which is a different posture from courage. Naming the aggressor by a type, and defining that type by disbelief in a reckoning, also makes a causal claim: arrogance of this kind rests on the assumption that no account will ever be given. Remove that assumption and the behaviour loses its ground.

crossReferences.why: The only other place this verb is used, spoken by Moses in nearly identical words.
Records the same accusation, of wanting to be a tyrant in the land rather than a reformer.
The threat this sentence answers, delivered as a fear for religion and for public order.

studies.applyIt: When you next face someone who has decided against you and holds more power, try the two halves of this sentence. Say where you have put yourself for safety, and describe the person by the type rather than by their name. Doing both keeps the fear accurate and stops the situation turning into a private feud inside your head.

studies.title: If He Is A Liar
studies.meaning: A man of Pharaoh's own household, who had kept his faith hidden, speaks for the first time, and what he offers is an argument anyone in the room could check. Are you killing a man for saying my Lord is God, when he has brought you clear proofs? Then a clean disjunction: if he is lying, the lie falls on him; if he is truthful, some of what he warns of will reach you. Commentators note that he never asserts Moses is right. He asks what a reasonable person does before knowing.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The Quran does not name this man, and one of the surah's two common titles comes from the phrase describing him. The commentators discuss his identity without reaching agreement and leave the anonymity of the text standing. The passage is addressed to a community in Mecca in which several believers were concealing their faith from their own families, and it shows one such person choosing his moment.

keyTerms.note: The phrase occurs once in the Quran. The verb means to hold something back rather than to deny it, so what is described is a silence maintained rather than a false statement made.
Things that make a matter plain, used of evidence that settles a dispute. He puts this on the record before drawing any conclusion at all, which is how his whole argument is built.
From a root meaning to pass a limit, used of overspending and of overreaching. It appears three times in this surah, and all three of them fall inside this man's speech.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Speaking against a ruler in his own court was not free debate but a calculation about survival. A courtier who dissented risked his position, his household and his life, and the safest form of dissent was procedural: not that the ruler is wrong, but that the proposed action is imprudent. That is the form this man chooses, and an audience in Mecca would have recognised it at once as the careful one.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran never gives this man a name; he is identified only as a believing man of Pharaoh's family who was concealing his faith, and one of this surah's two common titles comes from that description. The word he uses for going to excess occurs three times in the surah, and every one falls within his own words.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The argument is a model of reasoning under uncertainty, and scripture preserves it as such. He does not demand that they believe. He asks them to notice that one branch of the disjunction costs them nothing and the other costs them everything. Putting this in the mouth of a man who has hidden his own conviction also separates two things usually merged: what he privately holds, and what he can publicly establish.

crossReferences.why: Records another man from the same court coming with a warning, telling Moses to leave the city.
Gives a matching figure, a man from the far side of a city urging his people to follow the messengers.
The same speaker later drops the caution and openly calls his people to follow him.

studies.applyIt: Take a disagreement where you are fairly sure you are right, and try making the case as a fair disjunction instead: if this is wrong, here is who bears the cost; if it is right, here is what follows. Say it out loud once before you next speak. It is slower than asserting, and it is much harder to wave away.

studies.title: Who Will Help Us Then
studies.meaning: The address turns from the accused to the powerful. My people, the kingdom is yours today, uppermost in the land, but who will help us against God's force if it comes? He puts himself inside the question, which is the first hint of where he stands. Pharaoh's answer is quoted straight away and answers nothing: I show you only what I see, and I guide you only to the path of good sense. Commentators read the reply as authority reasserted in the costume of advice.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in a city whose leadership answered challenges in exactly this register. The man's question concedes the present arrangement completely and asks only about its durability, which was the harder question for Mecca as well. The phrase Pharaoh uses for the path of good sense returns later in this surah in the believer's own mouth, and the commentators note the collision as deliberate.

keyTerms.note: From a verb meaning both to appear and to overcome, related to the word for a back. It describes being visibly on top, which is precisely the form of power the question then tests.
A word for severity and fighting strength, used of hardship and of military power. It names God's action in the vocabulary of the one thing these particular men respected.
Sound judgement rather than piety, the quality of a person who chooses well. The phrase occurs twice in the Quran, both times in this surah, once here and once from the believer.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A ruler's answer to a hard question was often a display rather than an argument. In an assembly, saying that you tell people only what you judge best was a way of closing a discussion by restating who decides. Everyone present understood the move. The audience in Mecca had watched their own leaders end debates in the same manner, so the surah quotes it without explaining it.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase for the path of good sense occurs twice in the whole Quran, and both occurrences are in this surah. Here it is Pharaoh claiming to lead his people along it; nine ayat later the believing man uses the identical phrase for what he is offering. The dispute is fought, in part, over the ownership of one expression.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The question asked is not whether the powerful are wrong but whether they are covered. Power is granted, dominance is granted, and only the contingency is raised. That is an unusually modest form of challenge and considerably harder to dismiss than an accusation. Pharaoh's reply then demonstrates what authority does with a question it cannot answer: it restates itself, and calls the restatement guidance.

crossReferences.why: The believer takes this same phrase, the path of good sense, and applies it to what he offers instead.
Describes an earlier people who followed the command of every obstinate tyrant to their ruin.
Answers the same question historically, pointing at people who were stronger and had no protector.

studies.applyIt: Think of an arrangement in your life that is working well, and put this ayah's question to it without deciding anything: if this stops, who helps. Not as anxiety, and not to prompt action today. The man speaking here concedes that everything is fine at present. His question is only about the part nobody has planned for.

studies.title: O My People, I Fear For You
studies.meaning: Three sentences, each opening with the same address. My people, I fear for you a day like the day of the allied parties; like the settled way of the people of Noah and of two Arabian peoples and those after them; and God intends no injustice to His servants. My people, I fear for you the Day of Calling Out. Commentators note that he never says I fear you, only I fear for you, and that the middle clause defends God's justice while he is warning them of ruin.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The believer speaking stands inside Pharaoh's household and addresses the court as his own people, a form the Quran keeps through his whole speech. The examples he chooses are the ones the Quran cites to its Meccan audience: an earlier flood, and two Arabian civilisations whose remains lay along the trade routes. The commentators read the list as chosen for the surah's hearers as much as for the court.

keyTerms.note: A vocative with a possessive ending, so it claims them as his own. He repeats it through the speech, and it is the same form prophets use to address their communities throughout the Quran.
A noun for a persistent practice, from a verb meaning to keep at something. Applied to earlier peoples it names not their punishment but the settled behaviour that led them there.

keyTerms.gloss: the calling out to one another
keyTerms.note: A verbal noun of a form meaning mutual action, so people calling to each other rather than being summoned. It occurs once in the Quran, and commentators picture crowds calling across distance.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Kinship language did political work. Opening with my people bound a speaker to his audience and made criticism sound like counsel from inside rather than an attack from outside. A man who dropped that address had declared himself separate. In a court where the wrong word was fatal, keeping the possessive in place was not decoration; it was the structure that allowed the rest of the sentence to be said at all.
studies.didYouKnow: The Day named at the end of this passage, the Day of Calling Out, occurs once in the whole Quran. So does the phrase in the first sentence about the day of the allied parties. Both are names for the same event, and both fall inside this one short speech, which makes this passage the source of two of the Quran's rarest names for the Day.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The middle sentence carries the weight. Having listed peoples who were destroyed, he says at once that God intends no injustice to His servants, which stops the warning from becoming a portrait of arbitrary power. History is offered as consequence rather than as caprice. The repeated address then achieves what the argument alone could not: it establishes that the warning comes from someone who will share the outcome.

crossReferences.why: Names the same allied parties earlier in this surah, there in the surah's own voice.
Shows another warner addressing his people in the same form and with the same declared concern.
Ends this same speech, where he commits his own case to God once the warnings are finished.

studies.applyIt: The next time you warn someone you love, notice whether your sentence contains the word for. I fear for you is a different sentence from I am afraid of what you are doing, and people hear the difference immediately. Say the first version once this week, in those words, to someone who has stopped listening to the second.

studies.title: You Said No Messenger After Him
studies.meaning: The warning ends with a day of turning and fleeing with no protector anywhere, and then the speech turns to history the court itself owned. Joseph came to you before with clear proofs, and you never stopped doubting what he brought; and when he died you said God will never send a messenger after him. Commentators note the precision of the charge. They did not reject Joseph once he was gone. They promoted him, and used his standing to close the door on anyone arriving later.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The reference is to the Joseph of the Quran's twelfth surah, whose story the Meccan audience had been given at length not long before. The believer is reminding a court in Egypt of its own earlier history, which lets the surah make a point about how communities handle the messengers of the past: doubted while alive, then made final once safely dead. No occasion is reported.
