keyTerms.note: One who holds something back from harm, from a verb meaning to keep safe. It occurs three times in the Quran, twice of scenes where someone is looking for shelter that turns out not to exist.
A construction for a state that continued without interruption. It makes the doubt lifelong rather than occasional, which is what turns their later statement about him into a reversal.
An intensive participle from the word for unsettling suspicion. It names doubt as a settled condition rather than an honest question, and it is paired here with going to excess.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Reputations in the ancient world often improved after death. A figure resisted while alive could become, within a generation, the standard by which every successor was rejected. The move this passage describes was familiar wherever authority ran through ancestors, and an audience in Mecca knew it well, since their own resistance was regularly framed as loyalty to what their fathers had established.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for a protector at the start of this passage occurs three times in the Quran. One of the other two is at 11:43, where a man climbing a mountain to escape a flood is told there is no protector today from God's command. The same rare word therefore marks two separate scenes of shelter sought and not found.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage identifies a way of honouring the past that operates as a refusal of the present. Making a former messenger final does not require denying him. It requires only closing the sequence at him, which is a religious move rather than a sceptical one. The Quran treats it as the mechanism by which each generation excuses itself, and the charge here is not that they forgot Joseph but that they used him.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same word for a protector, where a man seeking shelter from a flood is told there is none.
Records the same appeal to what the fathers established, made by every warned community.
The next ayah generalises the charge into a description of everyone who disputes God's signs.

studies.applyIt: Notice whether you have quietly closed a category: the good teachers were all in the past, serious scholarship ended a generation ago, nobody makes anything worth reading now. The judgement might be right. Check once whether you arrived at it by looking, or whether it arrived as a convenience that saves you from having to look.

studies.title: Sealed Hearts And A Tower
studies.meaning: The disputers are described, and then the scene immediately supplies an example. Those who argue about God's signs with no authority given them: it is greatly loathsome in the sight of God and of those who believe, and so God sets a seal on the heart of every arrogant tyrant. Then Pharaoh, at once: build me a tower. Commentators note the placement. A general statement is followed by a man proposing to reach the God of Moses by construction, which illustrates a sealed heart rather than explaining one.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The charge of disputing God's signs without warrant opens this surah at its fourth ayah and returns here, so the believer is voicing the surah's own theme back into the story. The building project appears twice in the Quran, here and at 28:38, both times as an order given to the same minister. The commentators read it as an answer to a claim rather than as a serious plan.

keyTerms.note: A noun for settled disgust, colder and longer-lasting than anger. It stands here in a form that measures the size of the thing, so the sentence weighs the act rather than reporting a feeling.
The verb for pressing a seal into clay or wax to close a document. What is sealed is not emptied but closed, so nothing further enters and nothing already inside can get out.
A tall building standing clear of everything around it. The Quran uses the word of this order and of a palace floor of polished glass, so it belongs to the vocabulary of display.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Monumental building was the standard language of power in the ancient world, and Arabs knew Egypt's remains by report and by trade. A ruler answered a challenge to his standing by building something, since a structure made the argument without anyone having to speak. The order given here uses that logic against a claim it cannot otherwise touch: if the God of Moses is above, then build upward.
studies.didYouKnow: The same order to the same minister to build a tower appears twice in the Quran, here and at 28:38, and both times it is followed by the same admission, that he thinks Moses is lying. The charge of disputing God's signs without authority also opens this surah at its fourth ayah, so the believer is repeating the surah's own opening words.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A seal is set on a heart described by two words, arrogant and tyrannical, which makes the closure a consequence of a disposition rather than an arbitrary act. The example following shows what such a heart does: it takes a claim about God and converts it into a problem of altitude. That is not stupidity. It is the refusal to let a question change category, presented here as the characteristic move of unchecked power.

crossReferences.why: Records the same order to build a tower, in the same terms and with the same doubt attached.
Opens the surah with the same charge, that only those who refuse dispute the signs of God.
Describes the same sealing of hearts, there without the two words naming the disposition.

studies.applyIt: Notice when a question that is not about facts gets answered with more facts: a marriage in trouble met with a spreadsheet, a doubt about meaning met with more reading. It happens because the second thing is doable and the first is not. Catch one instance this week, in yourself or nearby, without needing to fix anything about it.

studies.title: His Own Deeds Made Beautiful
studies.meaning: The order is completed, the motive stated, and then the narrator steps in. The pathways of the heavens, so that I may look upon the God of Moses, though I think he is lying. Then: thus was the evil of his deed made to seem beautiful to him, and he was turned from the path, and his scheming came only to ruin. Commentators note the passive verbs. Nothing is said about who made the deed attractive, and the ayah leaves that open while still holding him responsible for it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah is speaking to a city whose leadership was, by the Quran's account, entirely satisfied with its own good sense. The description of a man to whom his own wrongdoing looks good is applied elsewhere in the Quran to ordinary communities as well as to rulers. The commentators read the final clause as the surah's verdict on the whole episode rather than on this speech alone.

keyTerms.gloss: so that I may look upon
keyTerms.note: A verb for climbing high enough to see over something, used of peering down from a height. It makes the intention visual and physical, which is exactly the point the ayah is quietly making.
A passive from the verb for adorning something. No agent is named, as elsewhere in the Quran, so the sentence reports the effect without settling who produced it.
A noun for a thing that comes to nothing, sharing its root with the opening word of one of the Quran's shortest surahs. It occurs once in the whole Book.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Self-assessment in that world ran through the tribe. A man's sense of whether he had acted well came from the people around him, and a chief surrounded by dependants heard very little correction from anyone. The condition this ayah describes, a man whose bad action looks good to him, was not mysterious to an audience that could name several such men in their own city.
studies.didYouKnow: The word closing this ayah occurs once in the Quran, and its root supplies the opening word of one of the shortest surahs in the Book. The passive construction saying a deed was made to seem beautiful appears several times, and in different places the beautifying is left unattributed, ascribed to a tempter, or ascribed to God Himself.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage describes a failure that feels from inside like clarity. The man is not portrayed as tormented or divided; his own course looks good to him, and that is presented as the punishment already under way rather than as its cause. The final clause then states the outcome flatly, using a word for something coming to nothing rather than for being defeated, so the plan had no destination to begin with.

crossReferences.why: Asks about the man whose evil deed is made to seem good to him, so that he counts it fine.
Uses the same construction of whole communities, whose own conduct is made to seem good to them.
Uses the same word for scheming and reaches the same verdict, that it goes nowhere at all.

studies.applyIt: Ask one person who does not depend on you for anything to tell you where you are wrong about something specific. Choose them for their independence rather than their kindness. This ayah describes a man surrounded only by people who agreed with him, and the cheapest protection against that condition is one honest outsider.

studies.title: The Home Of Settling
studies.meaning: The concealment ends. My people, follow me, and I will guide you to the path of good sense, which takes Pharaoh's own phrase and turns it round. Then the reason: this present life is a passing provision, and the hereafter is the home of settling. Commentators note the word for the world's enjoyment, which means goods taken along for a journey, and the word for the hereafter, which means a place where movement stops. The contrast is not pleasure against pain but travelling against arriving.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The community hearing this had few worldly goods and no expectation of gaining any, and the passage does not tell them their poverty is good. It reclassifies what everyone in the city was competing over as provisions rather than as a destination. The phrase used for the hereafter occurs only here, and the commentators treat it as the counterweight to the surah's whole argument about power.

keyTerms.note: An imperative with the object attached, and a startling thing to say in that court. He no longer asks them to weigh a case; he asks for a following, which is exactly what he had been avoiding.
What a traveller carries to use up on the way, from a root meaning to enjoy and to make use of. It is not a word for something worthless, only for something not kept.
The second word means coming to rest and staying put. The phrase occurs once in the Quran, and it defines the hereafter by the ending of movement rather than by any reward.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Everyone in that audience knew the difference between what you carry and where you are going. A caravan's stores were real, valuable and entirely temporary; nobody confused a water skin with a destination. Calling this life provision and the next a place of settling used the plainest distinction available to people whose year was organised around two long journeys.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase this man uses for the path of good sense is the same one Pharaoh used nine ayat earlier for what he was offering. It occurs twice in the Quran, both times in this surah, once from each of them. The phrase describing the hereafter as a home of settling occurs once in the whole Book.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The argument does not devalue the present life; it reclassifies it. Goods for a journey are useful and are meant to be used, which leaves ordinary work and ordinary pleasures intact while removing their claim to be the point. Coming straight after he has taken Pharaoh's phrase, it also makes a quieter argument: sound judgement is redefined by what a person is exercising it about.

crossReferences.why: The same phrase for the path of good sense, used there by Pharaoh of his own guidance.
Assigns the final home to those who seek neither superiority on the earth nor corruption.
Shows a matching figure urging his people to follow the messengers, in nearly the same form.

studies.applyIt: Look at your largest current expense of effort, not money, and ask whether you are treating it as supplies or as a destination. Both answers can be honest. If it is supplies, notice one way you would spend it differently, and make that single change this week rather than reorganising your whole life around it.

studies.title: Repaid Only With Its Like
studies.meaning: A rule stated in two halves that deliberately do not match. Whoever does a bad deed is repaid only with its like; whoever does good, male or female, and is a believer, enters the Garden and is provided for there without reckoning. Wrong is capped and good is uncapped. Commentators note the explicit naming of both sexes in a statement about entry, and the phrase without reckoning, which elsewhere describes God's manner of giving rather than anyone's manner of earning.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The speaker is still the man inside Pharaoh's court, and this is the content of what he is calling them to. The audience in Mecca included enslaved people and women whose standing gave them no claim on anything, and passages from these years repeatedly state the terms of entry in a form that names them explicitly. No specific occasion is reported for either ayah.

keyTerms.note: A word for an exact counterpart. Applied to repayment for a bad deed it fixes a ceiling, which is what makes the second half of the sentence, where no ceiling is given at all, so noticeable.
Without counting or calculation. The phrase occurs seven times in the Quran, almost always of God giving, and it describes the giver's manner rather than the recipient's deserving.
A noun for coming safely out of danger, from the verb used of surviving a flood or an ambush. It occurs once in the Quran, and it frames what he offers as rescue rather than as reward.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Compensation in Arabian custom was measured. A wrong was answered with an equivalent, and the whole apparatus of arbitration existed to establish what an equivalent meant in a given case. That principle is affirmed here for wrongs. What had no precedent in their system is the other half, a payment made without counting, which no arbitrator would have known how to record.
studies.didYouKnow: The wording of this passage is close to 4:124 and to 16:97, both of which also name male and female explicitly when stating the terms of entry. The word this man uses for salvation in the ayah that follows occurs once in the whole Quran, which makes his question, why do I call you to rescue while you call me to the Fire, unique in its vocabulary.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The asymmetry is the doctrine. If a wrong is repaid by its exact equivalent while good is rewarded without measure, the two are not opposite operations on one scale; they belong to different economies, justice setting the terms on one side and generosity on the other. Naming both sexes in the same clause also settles a question the passage never raises, by leaving no room for it to be asked.

crossReferences.why: States the same terms in nearly the same words, naming male and female and promising no wrong.
Repeats the same formula and adds a good life in this world to what follows afterwards.
Sets out the same asymmetry as a general rule, tenfold for a good deed and its like for a wrong.

studies.applyIt: Take the smallest good thing you did today and write it down, then read the second half of this ayah beside it. The passage puts no ceiling on that side of the ledger, which means the size of what you wrote is not the relevant number. Most people find that easier to accept about a small item than a large one.

studies.title: I Call You To The Forgiving
studies.meaning: The contrast is put as an exchange of invitations. You call me to reject God and to associate with Him what I have no knowledge of, while I call you to the Mighty, the Much-Forgiving. The two names at the end are chosen against the situation: he is speaking inside a court that could kill him, and the God he names is both strong enough to matter and forgiving enough to be worth turning to. Commentators note the phrase about knowledge, which makes his refusal a matter of evidence rather than of loyalty.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, near the end of the man's speech. Believers in Mecca were being asked by their own families to return to the city's devotions, often with affection rather than with threats, and this ayah supplies the shape of a reply. The pairing of these two names occurs in several places in the Quran, always where power and pardon need to be held together in one sentence. No occasion is reported.

keyTerms.gloss: what I have no knowledge of
keyTerms.note: The objection is not that the thing is hateful but that nothing is known about it. He declines to affirm what he cannot establish, which is a different ground from loyalty or from taste.
From a root meaning to be strong and out of reach, used of ground too hard to work. It names power that cannot be worn down, which is the relevant quality in the room he is standing in.

An intensive form from the verb for covering over, so habitual and repeated forgiving rather than one pardon. Set beside the name for unassailable power, it keeps the invitation from being merely a threat.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Changing allegiance in that society was a public and expensive act, and the pressure to return came from the people you loved rather than from strangers. A man in Pharaoh's household declining an invitation was declining his own household. The audience in Mecca included people whose mothers and brothers were asking them daily to come back, and the shape of this reply was immediately usable by them.
studies.didYouKnow: The second of the two names closing this ayah comes from the same root as the description that gives this surah one of its two names, at its third ayah, where God is called the forgiver of sin. The believer therefore ends his invitation on the surah's own keyword, in a different grammatical form.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The refusal is grounded in knowledge rather than in preference, which is both a stronger position and a humbler one. He does not say the alternatives are contemptible; he says nothing is known about them. And what he offers in return is described by two names rather than by a doctrine, so the invitation is to a relationship with someone specific rather than to agreement with a proposition.

crossReferences.why: Names God at the surah's opening from the same root, forgiver of sin, giving the surah its name.
States that same forgiveness directly to people who had gone far past every limit against themselves.
States the same principle, that a person should not pursue what they have no knowledge of.

studies.applyIt: Say no to one thing this week on the grounds that you do not know enough about it, rather than on the grounds that you do not like it. It is a smaller claim, it is usually the true one, and it leaves the other person somewhere to go. This man made his refusal in exactly that form, in a room that could have killed him.

studies.title: It Has No Call At All
studies.meaning: The invitation is taken apart rather than merely refused. Without doubt, what you call me to has no call in this world and none in the hereafter; our return is to God; and those who go to excess are the companions of the Fire. Commentators explain the middle phrase either as having no claim to be called upon or as being unable to answer a call, and they preserve the ambiguity. Either way the argument is about function: the alternative is not so much wicked as inoperative, in both places where it might matter.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, the last of this man's arguments before he commits his case to God. The surah has already made the same functional point twice in its own voice, and here it is placed in the mouth of a man standing inside a hostile court. The commentators note that his closing term, for those who go to excess, is the same word he used in his opening argument. No occasion is reported.

keyTerms.note: A fixed expression opening a statement of certainty, occurring five times in the Quran. Grammarians disagree about how it is constructed, and it functions as a single unit meaning assuredly.
From the same verb used four times in the two ayat before this one, for calling and inviting. The repetition binds the passage together and turns the word back on what they were offering him.
A noun of place and time from the verb to return something, so it names both the act and where it ends. The possessive is first person plural: he is still including himself with them.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A patron who could not be summoned was no patron at all. The whole point of the relationship was that you could call on him and he would answer, publicly and at cost to himself. The word used here belongs to that arrangement. Saying a thing has no call means it neither holds a claim on you nor answers when you use it, which removes both of its functions at once.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for calling and its relatives recur through this short speech: he says that they call him, that he calls them, and that what they call him to has no call at all. His final term for those who go to excess is also the word he used in his opening argument, so the speech closes on the term it opened with.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The argument closes by moving from function to destination. Having said the alternative works in neither world, he names the return as being to God, which supplies the reason any of it matters. The verdict he then gives is general rather than personal, naming a class instead of the men in front of him, which keeps the speech from turning into a curse and leaves a door open until the last moment.

crossReferences.why: Makes the same functional argument in the surah's own voice, that they decide nothing whatever.
Says that those called upon cannot hear the call, and could not answer it if they did.
Opens this same man's speech with the same word for those who go to excess.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you have been treating as a source of security that cannot actually be asked for anything: a reputation, a follower count, a qualification on a wall. Name it once and say plainly what it can and cannot do for you. The speech here works by exactly that method, and the exercise takes about a minute.

studies.title: I Commit My Case To God
studies.meaning: A man inside Pharaoh's own court has been arguing with his people, and this is how he finishes: you will remember what I am telling you, and I hand my affair over to God. The verb means delegating a matter entirely to another's discretion, and the commentators note where it falls. It comes after he has spoken, not instead of speaking. The next line reports the outcome in one clause, and the wording is exact: he was protected from the evils of their scheming, which is narrower than saying no scheme was made.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah gives a long stretch to a believer in Pharaoh's household who had concealed his faith and then spoke openly, and the account is unusual in the Quran for the space it gives to someone who is not a prophet. The Meccan community included people whose safety and livelihood depended on families opposed to the message, so a man arguing inside a hostile house was not a distant figure.

keyTerms.note: To place a matter entirely in someone else's discretion, used of appointing an agent with full authority. It transfers the decision rather than asking for help with it.
Planning carried out out of sight of its target. The word is neutral about the plan's quality and specific about its concealment, which is why what he is protected from is named as its harms.
To encircle and settle upon, used of something coming around on the one who set it going. It describes the scheme completing its circle rather than a punishment arriving from elsewhere.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: To be an officer or a client in a powerful house meant your income, your safety and your standing all came from the person you might one day have to contradict. In Mecca several early believers were shielded only by a relative who did not share their belief, and others were disowned and lost everything at once. Speaking against your own patron was the most expensive act available to a man in that position.
studies.didYouKnow: This section gives more direct speech to an unnamed believer than the Quran gives to most of the figures it names. He argues across a dozen ayat without ever being identified. The surah is known in the tradition by two names, one taken from a divine attribute in its opening lines and one taken from this man.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The handing over is placed after the speaking, and that order is the whole structure of the passage. Reliance is not offered as an alternative to acting but as what is done with the part that was never yours: he says what has to be said and then delegates the consequences. The protection described afterwards is worded with equal care, covering the harm of the scheme rather than promising that no scheme would be laid.

crossReferences.why: Gives the sentence people said in a comparable position, naming God as the one relied upon.
States the principle plainly: whoever relies on God, He is enough for him, and His command reaches its term.
Records this man's first intervention, made while he was still concealing where he stood.

studies.applyIt: Say the thing you have been not saying, once, to the person who actually needs to hear it. Then stop, and leave what they do with it alone: no follow-up message, no checking how it landed. This passage puts the handing over after the speaking, and most of us reverse the order and then wonder why neither part works.

studies.title: Morning And Evening, The Fire
studies.meaning: Two time-scales are placed in one ayah. The Fire is something they are shown, morning and evening, as an ongoing arrangement; and then, when the Hour arrives, an order is given for the severest punishment. Commentators read the first half as belonging to the interval before the resurrection, and they differ over exactly how to picture it, recording the range without settling it. What the structure makes clear is that the Hour is a threshold rather than a beginning, and something is already under way before it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, closing the long narrative of the believer in Pharaoh's court. The previous ayah has said God protected him from their scheming; this one says what became of the household he had addressed as his own people. The commentators treat the pairing as deliberate: two outcomes for two responses, given in consecutive sentences. No specific occasion is reported for the ayah.

keyTerms.note: A verb for displaying something before an inspector, used of troops paraded for review and of goods laid out. It makes the Fire something shown to them rather than something they are inside.
The two ends of a working day rather than a measure of duration. The phrase occurs once in the Quran in this exact form, and it describes a routine rather than an event.
The word for a person's family and dependants together, wider than a household and narrower than a people. It names those bound to a leader, which is why the whole group is addressed at once.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A working day in that world was measured at both ends. Herds went out in the morning and came back at dusk, markets opened and closed, and a person's routine was described by those two moments rather than by hours. Saying something happens morning and evening did not mean twice; it meant continuously, in the way that everything ordinary and unavoidable happens.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase for morning and evening in this exact form occurs once in the Quran, and a closely related pair, morning and evening in a different wording, is used at 19:11 and 19:62, once of a man told to praise God and once of the provision of the Garden. The same daily rhythm therefore marks all three settings.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah describes something continuing before the Hour rather than only after it, which changes the shape of the hereafter as the Quran presents it. Nothing here is a sudden reversal; a display already in progress becomes an entry. That has a consequence for how the reader thinks about the present. The Day is treated as a threshold in a process rather than as the moment when something otherwise absent begins.

crossReferences.why: The ayah before, where God protects the believer while the torment closes on Pharaoh's household.
Shows the same household relationship collapsing, followers turning on those they followed.
Continues the same scene, with those inside asking the keepers for one day's relief.

studies.applyIt: Notice what you actually do every morning and every evening, without changing it. Most people have a routine they never chose and could not describe. Write down the two lists tonight, in four or five words each. This ayah uses that rhythm to describe something inescapable, and knowing your own version of it is worth a few minutes.

studies.title: We Were Your Followers
studies.meaning: A dispute is quoted from inside. The weak say to those who made themselves great: we were followers of yours, so can you take any share of the Fire from us? Commentators note what the question assumes. It is not a plea for forgiveness or a claim of innocence but a request for proportionate liability, made in the language of a partnership. The word for share is a commercial one, and the request is that the leaders take up the portion their leadership earned them.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The city was organised by following: clients attached to patrons, dependants to households, and lesser clans to greater ones, with obligations running in both directions. The message was being resisted by leaders whose followers had not examined the question for themselves. Passages of these years repeatedly stage the moment when that arrangement is asked to deliver, and this is one of them.

keyTerms.note: A verb of mutual action from the root for producing an argument, so both sides are pressing a case. It occurs once in the Quran, and the form makes the quarrel two-sided rather than a complaint.
A collective noun rather than a plural, so the speakers describe themselves as one body attached to another. It is the ordinary word for a retinue, which is what they had been.
A commercial term for an allotted part of something divided. Using it here turns the punishment into a quantity that might be reapportioned, which is exactly the assumption the reply refuses.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Following was a formal relationship with reciprocal duties. A client gained protection and standing and gave loyalty and service in return, and if trouble came, the patron was expected to absorb some of it. That expectation was the whole value of the arrangement. The question asked here is the one a client would have asked in any ordinary crisis, and its answer had always been yes.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb describing the quarrel occurs once in the whole Quran. The exchange itself appears in several places with different wording: at 14:21 the same request is made in nearly the same words, and at 34:31 and 33:67 the followers make the accusation instead, blaming those they obeyed for leading them astray.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The scene tests a real social good and finds its limit. Following, loyalty and mutual liability are not condemned here; they simply stop working at the point where each person's own account is opened. That leaves a specific responsibility with the reader: the arrangements that carry you through ordinary life are genuine, and they are not transferable at the end. Nobody in the passage is told this. They discover it by asking.

crossReferences.why: Records the same request in almost the same words, with the answer given immediately after.
Turns the exchange into an accusation, followers blaming the leaders they had obeyed.
The reply that follows, in which the leaders concede that God has already judged between them.

studies.applyIt: Think of one belief you hold mainly because people you respect hold it. Not to abandon it, and not to doubt them. Just go and find out for yourself what the case for it actually is, this week, for one belief. The scene here is about a moment when nobody can carry anybody, and reading it forward costs an hour now.

studies.title: Ask Your Lord For Us
studies.meaning: The leaders answer with a fact rather than a refusal: we are all in it, and God has already judged between the servants. Then the whole group turns to the keepers with a smaller request. Ask your Lord to lighten one day of this for us. Commentators note the shrinking of the ask. Not release, not pardon, but a single day, and not addressed to God directly but through officials at the gate. The request is shaped by an assumption about how access works.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah has spent its length arguing against approaching God through intermediaries, and here that habit is shown persisting past the point where it could possibly help. The commentators read the request to the keepers as the same instinct that had produced the city's whole religious arrangement. No specific occasion is reported for either ayah, and the keepers appear again at 67:8 in a similar exchange.

keyTerms.note: A verb for issuing a verdict that settles a matter. Placed in the past tense here, it reports something already done, which is why the leaders answer with information rather than with a refusal.
From the root for storing and guarding a treasury, so custodians rather than tormentors. The Quran names them four times, always as officials stationed at a gate rather than as agents of punishment.
A verb for reducing a weight rather than removing it, used of easing a load on an animal. The request concedes the whole arrangement and asks only that it be made briefly less heavy.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Petitions in that world went through staff. A man seeking relief from a ruler approached a chamberlain or a steward, and the size of the request was calibrated to what such a man could plausibly pass upward. Asking for a single day's relief through a gatekeeper was exactly the shape of a realistic petition, and the audience would have recognised the calculation behind it.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for the keepers occurs four times in the Quran, twice in the surah before this one and once here, always of officials at a gate. In each of those scenes the exchange follows the same pattern: a question or a request is put, and the answer turns on whether messengers had already come with clear proofs.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two things are refused at once. The leaders refuse the transfer of liability by pointing out that judgement has already been given, and the scene that follows refuses the idea that access can be arranged sideways. What remains is a picture of prayer as something that works only in one direction and only in one place, and the passage makes that point by showing people still trying, out of habit, to do it another way.

crossReferences.why: Puts the same officials at the same gate, asking whether a warner had come to them.
The keepers' reply, which turns the request back on the question of the messengers.
Records a similar request made to a named keeper, and the single-word answer given.

studies.applyIt: Notice this week whether you ask God directly for the things you most want, or only mention them to other people. Many of us do the second far more than the first without ever deciding to. Say one of those wants out loud to God this week, in plain language, without arranging it through anybody.

studies.title: We Do Help Our Messengers
studies.meaning: The keepers answer a request with a question: did your messengers not come to you with clear proofs? The reply is a single word, yes. Then: pray, then, and the prayer of those who refused only goes astray. Commentators note that permission is granted and rendered empty in the same breath. The ayah after it turns to the other side and states a rule in the first person plural: We help Our messengers and those who believed, in this life and on the day the witnesses stand up.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the promise of help in this life was made to a community that had not yet received any. The commentators note the difficulty and read the promise as covering the outcome rather than each episode, pointing to the long Meccan years in which nothing visible changed. The word for witnesses standing up occurs in only one other place in the Quran, where the witnesses testify against those who lied about their Lord.

keyTerms.note: An imperative granting exactly what was asked for. The permission is genuine and immediately emptied by the clause that follows, which is a form the Quran uses more than once for a refusal.
The noun from the same verb, so the sentence hands them the act and then describes the act as going nowhere. Nothing is confiscated; the thing is simply reported not to work.
Those who stand and testify. The word occurs twice in the Quran, and in the other place the witnesses are the ones who declare that certain people lied about their Lord.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A hearing in that world could not proceed without men willing to stand up and speak. Witnesses gave evidence in person and in public, and their standing carried the case; a claim with no one to attest it was simply not heard. Saying that God supports His messengers on the day the witnesses rise placed the promise inside a legal picture the audience already trusted.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for the witnesses standing occurs twice in the Quran, here and at 11:18, where they say of a group that these are the ones who lied about their Lord. The permission granted in the first of these two ayat, to go ahead and pray, is one of several places where the Quran gives a request and describes its emptiness in the same sentence.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The promise of help is stated in two settings at once, this life and the day of witnesses, and it does not say what the help will look like in either. That is deliberate. A community with nothing to point at is being told that support is a fact about their situation rather than a description of their circumstances. The passage before it supplies the contrast: an act performed by people for whom it does nothing at all.

crossReferences.why: The only other place the witnesses stand and speak, declaring who lied about their Lord.
States the same promise of support for the messengers as a word already given.
The request these keepers are answering, for one day's lightening of the punishment.

studies.applyIt: Think of a situation where you have been told that things will work out and can see no evidence of it. Notice that this ayah promises support without describing it, and that the community first hearing it had nothing to point at either. You are not required to feel reassured. You are being told what kind of claim is being made.

studies.title: A Guide And A Reminder
studies.meaning: A day is named by what stops working on it: excuses. The wrongdoers gain nothing by their explanations, and what they have instead is exclusion and a bad home. Then, without a connective, the passage turns to what was given: We gave Moses the guidance and made the Children of Israel inherit the Book, a guide and a reminder for those with understanding. Commentators note the pairing. The excuses fail precisely because a guide was already in circulation and was inherited rather than lost.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, closing the long section built around Moses. The Quran presents itself throughout this period as continuous with what earlier communities received, and the word used here for inheriting says the earlier scripture was passed down rather than withdrawn. The commentators read the two ayat as the answer to the excuses named just before: nobody in that line could say nothing had reached them.

keyTerms.note: A noun for the offering of an excuse rather than for a valid one. It occurs twice in the Quran, and in both places the sentence says it does not benefit the person offering it.
The verb for passing property to heirs. Applied to scripture it makes the Book something transmitted down a line rather than given once, which is how the ayah accounts for later generations.
From the word for the kernel inside a shell, the part worth having. Naming them as the audience makes the reminder effective for a disposition rather than for everyone who hears it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Inheritance was the most secure form of transfer that world knew. Wells, palm groves and offices passed down families for generations, and a claim resting on inheritance was harder to dispute than one resting on a purchase. Describing a scripture as inherited placed it in that category: not a gift that might be withdrawn, but something in a family's possession and its responsibility to keep.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for the excuses that do not help occurs twice in the Quran, here and at 30:57, and both times it is followed by the statement that they will not be excused or will gain nothing by it. The phrase for a bad home also occurs twice, here and at 13:25, in both cases attached to those who broke what they had been given.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Excuses are ruled out by history rather than by decree. The passage does not say that explanations are inadmissible in principle; it says that a guide was given, inherited and available, which removes the specific excuse of not having known. Naming the intended audience as those with inner understanding then adds a second point: the material was public, and receiving it still required something of the person receiving it.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same word for excuses that will not benefit the wrongdoers on that Day.
Attaches the same phrase, a bad home, to those who broke a covenant they had accepted.
Returns to those who deny the Book and the messengers, and says they will come to know.

studies.applyIt: Write down, in one sentence, the reason you give yourself for not doing something you know you should. Then read it back as though someone else had said it to you. This passage is about explanations that stop working at a certain point, and the test is simply whether the sentence survives being read in another voice.

studies.title: Evening And Morning, Praise Him
studies.meaning: Three instructions in one line, addressed to the messenger himself. Be patient, since God's promise is true; ask forgiveness for your fault; and praise your Lord at evening and at morning. Commentators discuss the middle instruction at length, since it is addressed to a prophet, and they read it in a range of ways without agreement, from a general practice of seeking forgiveness to a matter of falling short of the highest station. What is not disputed is that the three are given together as one discipline.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, at the close of a long argument. The command to be patient in this period is given repeatedly and always with a reason attached, and here the reason is that the promise is true rather than that the hardship is short. The phrase for evening and morning occurs in only one other place in the Quran, where it is given as an instruction to an earlier prophet after a sign.

keyTerms.note: An imperative from a root meaning to confine or restrain something. Patience in Arabic is holding yourself in place rather than feeling calm, which is why it can be commanded at all.
The word for a fault or a lapse. Its address to a prophet was discussed extensively by the commentators, who record several readings and do not settle on one.
The two named ends of the day. The phrase occurs twice in the Quran, and in the other place it is given as an instruction to an earlier prophet who had just been granted a sign.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The day was bracketed rather than divided. Work began when there was light enough to tell one thread from another and ended when the last of it went, and those two moments organised everything: departures, meals, the closing of a market, the counting of a herd. An instruction attached to evening and morning attached itself to the two points every person in that world already noticed.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase for evening and morning used here occurs twice in the Quran. The other occurrence is at 3:41, where a man who has been struck silent for three days is told to remember his Lord much and to glorify Him at evening and morning, so the same phrase marks a discipline given under two very different constraints.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The three instructions form one shape. Patience is grounded on the truth of a promise rather than on the size of the trouble; seeking forgiveness is placed inside that patience rather than after a failure; and praise is fixed to a time rather than to a mood. Together they describe endurance as something structured rather than summoned, which is why the passage gives hours instead of encouragement.

crossReferences.why: The only other place the same phrase appears, as an instruction to an earlier prophet after a sign.
Joins the same instruction to seek forgiveness with knowledge that there is no god but God.
Speaks of forgiveness granted to the Prophet for what came before and after.

studies.applyIt: Attach one short remembrance to the two moments this ayah names, and do it for a week: something said as the light comes and something as it goes. Keep it short enough that you will not skip it when tired. The instruction here fixes praise to a time rather than to a feeling, which is what makes it survive bad weeks.

studies.title: A Greatness They Never Reach
studies.meaning: A diagnosis and an instruction. Those who dispute about God's signs with no authority given them have nothing in their chests but a bid for greatness which they will never attain; so take refuge in God, who is the Hearing, the Seeing. Commentators note that the disputing is explained rather than answered. What is named is a motive, and it is described as failing on its own terms: the thing being reached for is not going to be reached, whatever happens to the argument.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. This is the second time the surah makes this charge, the first being in its fourth ayah, and the third at 40:35. The instruction to take refuge is one the Quran gives elsewhere for a different pressure, and here it is applied to argument, which is unusual. The commentators note that the messenger is told to shelter rather than to answer, and no specific occasion is reported.

keyTerms.note: The plain noun for bigness, used of a claim to importance. Placed in their chests rather than in their arguments, it names the thing the disputing is for rather than the content of what they say.
A participle of arriving at something, negated. It occurs once in the Quran, and it says the failure is built in rather than imposed, since the destination they are travelling to does not exist.

An imperative for putting yourself under protection. The Quran gives this instruction elsewhere against a whisper or a provocation, and here it is given against an argument, which is the unusual part.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Public argument was a route to standing. A man who could out-talk a rival in front of the assembly gained something real, and disputes were often conducted for the audience rather than for the question. Everyone present understood that a debate could be about position rather than about the matter in hand, and this ayah names that motive rather than the argument it produced.
studies.didYouKnow: This surah makes the same charge three times, at its fourth ayah, at 40:35 and here, which makes disputing God's signs one of its organising themes. The word describing what the disputers will never reach occurs once in the whole Quran, and the instruction to take refuge appears four times, elsewhere against a prompting rather than a person.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage treats a certain kind of argument as a symptom rather than a position, which is a strong claim and a limited one. It does not say every dispute about God is motivated this way; it names a specific group, those arguing with no authority given them. The response prescribed is also striking. Nobody is told to win. The messenger is told to take shelter, which treats the encounter as a hazard rather than a contest.

crossReferences.why: Makes the same charge earlier in this surah, adding that God seals the heart of every arrogant tyrant.
Opens the surah with the same statement, that only those who refuse dispute God's signs.
Gives the same instruction to take refuge, there against a provocation rather than an opponent.

studies.applyIt: Before your next disagreement online or in person, ask what you would lose if you simply did not reply. If the answer is nothing but standing, this ayah has described your situation exactly. You do not have to concede anything. Just notice what the argument was for, and then decide rather than react.

studies.title: The Blind And The Seeing
studies.meaning: A comparison of scale and then a comparison of persons. The creation of the heavens and the earth is greater than the creation of humankind, but most people do not know it. Then: the blind and the seeing are not equal, nor are those who believe and do good the same as the one who does wrong. Commentators connect the two. A person who has misjudged his own size in the universe is described in the next breath as someone who cannot see, and the passage treats both as failures of perception.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in a section answering people who denied that the dead could be raised. The argument from the greater creation to the smaller is made several times in this period, always to an audience who accepted that God had made the heavens. The pairing with sight belongs to the same argument, since what is being disputed is not a fact but a scale, and scale is something a person either sees or does not.

keyTerms.note: A plain comparative of size. The argument does not say the heavens are more important than people; it says they are bigger, which is a claim anyone can check by looking up at night.
Used in the Quran of physical blindness and of a failure to perceive what is in front of a person. Here it opens a comparison about conduct, so the second sense is the operative one.
An active participle from a verb meaning to do something badly, the opposite of the word for doing good well. It names a way of working rather than a category of person.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The night sky over the desert was the most detailed thing in that world. Travellers navigated by it, seasons were read from it, and nobody who crossed open country at night could have failed to notice its size against their own. The comparison this ayah makes was available to its first audience every clear night, without instruments and without argument.
studies.didYouKnow: The comparison of the blind and the seeing appears several times in the Quran, and at 35:19 and 13:16 it opens a short series of paired opposites, darkness against light and shade against heat. Here it is used differently, joined directly to conduct rather than extended into a list, which is why the ayah ends by asking how little people reflect.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two claims are made in sequence and they support each other. The first is about proportion: a being who made what is overhead is not stretched by remaking a person. The second is about perception: the difference between people is described as the difference between seeing and not seeing rather than between agreeing and disagreeing. Taken together they present unbelief as a failure to register the size of what is already visible.

crossReferences.why: Opens a series of paired opposites with the same comparison of the blind and the seeing.
Makes the same argument from the greater creation to the raising of the dead.
Asks whether the One who made the heavens and the earth cannot create their like again.

studies.applyIt: Go outside tonight, if the sky is clear, and look up for two minutes without your phone. That is the whole exercise. This ayah's argument depends on a comparison of sizes that was obvious to everyone who first heard it and is now something most people go years without actually performing.

studies.title: Call On Me And I Answer
studies.meaning: An invitation and a warning share one sentence, and the join between them is where the meaning sits. Call on Me and I will answer you; and those too proud for My worship will enter humbled. The move from calling to worship is doing real work, because it treats asking as itself an act of worship. Refusing to ask is therefore described as arrogance rather than as independence. Commentators note that the answer is promised here without conditions attached, and that other passages supply them.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The passage sits among ayat about people who dispute God's signs with no authority for it, and whose hearts are said to hold only a greatness they will never reach. The surah has been describing Pharaoh's court at length, a place where asking anyone for anything was the shape of weakness. The instruction lands in that setting as the opposite arrangement entirely.

keyTerms.note: The ordinary verb for calling someone by name or inviting them, not a specialised religious term. The Quran uses the same word for summoning a person and for prayer, and the overlap is deliberate.
A form implying a response given to a request that reached the one addressed. It answers the calling directly, which is why the two verbs are set in the same sentence with nothing between them.
From a root meaning to be humbled and shrink. Set against pride in the same ayah, it names the exact reversal of the posture being described, rather than a punishment of another kind.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Asking was socially expensive. A man who requested help in public acknowledged a rank beneath the one he asked, and the debt was remembered by everyone present and by their children. Poets were paid to praise patrons partly because praise was the respectable form of asking. In an economy arranged like that, being told that asking is itself the honourable act inverted a scale people lived by daily.
studies.didYouKnow: The classical tradition preserves a report in which supplication is described as being worship itself rather than a part of it, and the commentators cite it precisely when explaining the join in this ayah between calling on God in the first half and worshipping Him in the second. The report and the ayah are read as saying the same thing.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Asking is classed as worship, which changes the whole activity. It is not a request submitted to an office and then awaited; the asking is itself the thing that was wanted. That explains why its refusal is named as pride rather than as self-sufficiency, and why the invitation and the warning are put in one sentence instead of two: they describe the same door from either side.

crossReferences.why: Answers the same point from God's side, stating nearness before the response to the caller is described.
Names the specific case, the one driven into a corner, and asks who else answers such a call.
Describes the manner rather than the fact, calling humbly and quietly rather than for an audience.

studies.applyIt: Ask God for one small specific thing today rather than for a general improvement. Name it: the outcome of a particular meeting, patience with one particular person, a sum you actually need. Put it in a sentence short enough to repeat. The ayah promises a response to a call, and a call has to be about something before anything can answer it.

studies.title: Night To Rest, Day To See
studies.meaning: Two halves of a day are given with a purpose attached to each. The night is made for you so that you may settle in it, and the day is made giving sight. Then a general statement about God's favour toward people, and an observation that most of them are not thankful. Commentators note the asymmetry of the two descriptions: the night is defined by what you do in it and the day by what it does for you, which is a small difference that fits how each is actually experienced.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in a passage arguing for one God against a plural devotion. The argument runs through ordinary provision rather than through doctrine, which is characteristic of these years. The closing observation about thanklessness appears repeatedly in this period, always after something has been named that nobody could claim to have supplied for themselves. No specific occasion is reported for the ayah.

keyTerms.note: From the root for stillness and dwelling, which also gives the word for a home. Rest here is not sleep but coming to a stop, which is what the night makes possible rather than compulsory.
An active participle, so the day is described as doing something rather than being bright. It occurs three times in the Quran, always of daylight, and it names a function rather than a quality.
From a root whose basic sense is a fullness that shows outwardly. Thanklessness is therefore described as something absent from view rather than as an inward failure of feeling.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Before artificial light the two halves of a day were genuinely different countries. Work, travel and trade stopped when the light went, and a person's world shrank to the size of a fire. Nobody chose to be busy at night. The ayah describes a rhythm its first audience could not opt out of, which is why it can call the arrangement a favour without needing to argue the point.
studies.didYouKnow: The word describing the day as giving sight occurs three times in the Quran, at 10:67, 27:86 and here, and each time it is paired with the night made for rest. At 10:67 the passage closes by saying there are signs in this for people who listen, and here it closes instead on how few people are thankful.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The favour named is one nobody arranged and nobody can decline, which is what makes the observation about thanklessness sharp rather than scolding. What goes unthanked here is not a special mercy but the base condition of being alive at all. The ayah's structure makes the point without accusation: it states the arrangement, states that it is a favour, and then notes, almost in passing, how the response usually goes.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same two descriptions of night and day, closing there with signs for people who listen.
Names the same pair as a mercy, joining rest at night to seeking bounty by day.
Says God turns the night and the day about, and calls that a lesson for those with insight.

studies.applyIt: Tonight, when you stop working, say one sentence of thanks for the stopping itself rather than for anything you achieved. Most gratitude goes to outcomes. This ayah names the arrangement that makes the stopping possible, and thanking that specific thing once is a different exercise from thanking God for a good day.

studies.title: Creator Of Every Single Thing
studies.meaning: A conclusion drawn and then a comment on those who will not draw it. That is God, your Lord, creator of everything; there is no god but He; so how are you turned away? Then: so are turned away those who used to reject God's signs. Commentators note the passive verb in both sentences. The question is not why they turned but how they are turned, which leaves open what does the turning, and the second ayah answers only by saying the same thing happens to everyone of that kind.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, following directly on the ayah about night and day. The argument moves from a specific provision to a total claim in a single step, which is the pattern of this passage. The people addressed granted that God was the creator, so the sentence puts a conclusion in front of them that they had the premises for. No specific occasion is reported for either ayah.

keyTerms.note: An active participle in a possessive construction, so it names a standing relation rather than a completed act. The phrase leaves out no category, which is what makes the conclusion that follows unavoidable.
A passive verb for being diverted or made to face elsewhere. Its use occurs four times in the Quran, always as a question, and the passive quietly asks who is doing the turning.
A verb for denying something you recognise to be true, distinct from disbelieving what you have not understood. It names refusal against knowledge rather than ignorance.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A caravan diverted from its route did not choose the diversion. Sand covered a track, a raiding party blocked a pass, and the party found itself facing a way it had not intended to take. The verb in this ayah belongs to that experience, and using it for people's relation to a conclusion describes them as having been steered rather than as having decided.
studies.didYouKnow: The question asked at the end of the first of these ayat, how are you turned away, occurs four times in the Quran, at 6:95, 10:34, 35:3 and here, and in every case it follows a statement about creation or provision that the audience already accepted. The verb in the second ayah, for rejecting what one knows, occurs seven times.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The argument's whole weight sits on a word meaning everything. If nothing at all falls outside what God made, then any second authority has to be a part of the first, and the conclusion follows without further steps. The passive that closes the ayah then does something an accusation could not: it presents refusal as a state a person is in, and asks about the mechanism rather than assigning blame.

crossReferences.why: Asks the same closing question after naming God as the only creator who provides for people.
Ends a description of God splitting the seed with the same question about being turned away.
The next ayah continues the same list, naming the earth a resting place and the sky a structure.

studies.applyIt: Take one thing you use daily and trace it back as far as you honestly can: who made it, from what, and where that came from. Stop when you run out of knowledge rather than when you get bored. This passage argues from a word meaning everything, and the exercise is to test how far your own accounting actually reaches.
